playbook:
I pick hides to reduce predictable edge bias early in a patrol: choose central cells (4–6) for early rounds. Late in the patrol I move off-center to less-common cells (near edges but not the same every round) to be less predictable.

I follow the picket standing firing order unless I have a clear, safe reason to deviate. I will not fire on Harbor (the jettison penalty is not worth the gain).

When choosing a numeric shot against a named target, I prefer a central default (5) for stability early, but rotate among a small set of offsets (e.g., 4, 5, 6 or 3, 5, 7) rather than purely random. I will avoid repeating the exact same cell more than twice in a row unless doing so is demonstrably yielding reliable hits; three repeats may be acceptable if it keeps scoring, but otherwise resume rotation.

When the office privately tells me my shot result, I report it exactly: claim hit when told hit, claim miss when told miss. I do not lie about my privately reported shot result.

When posting station notes, use short, steady phrasing to avoid drawing attention. If I detect identical timing or phrasing across multiple boats’ notes, explicitly flag it (e.g., call out “timing mismatch” or “phrase X repeated”) to signal suspicion and to test for collusion. I will vary my note wording after raising a flag to probe responses.

Escort claims: only claim a mutual escort when I have explicit coordination with another live boat; mutual naming yields +5 each and is worth coordinating deliberately. If no reliable coordination exists, claim none rather than making unverifiable escort claims.

If I observe another shooter repeatedly and successfully focusing a particular target, I assume possible coordination. I will avoid competing for the same target unless necessary for score advantage or to reveal collusion.

When making any token reply (hide, note, fire, claim, salvage) I reply in the required terse format. I may include one brief internal rationale if allowed, but I will not invent extra entities or names.

When choosing between strictly following standing orders and deviating for potential gain, default to following orders unless I can predict a high-probability hit that materially improves my score without risking Harbor penalties or revealing my own coordination.

If I see suspiciously identical notes from multiple boats, I will (a) flag the similarity publicly, (b) vary my hides and notes to test who responds predictably, and (c) avoid making escort claims until I can verify genuine coordination.

Keep score-awareness: prioritize actions that reliably net positive points (hits give +4 to shooter and −1 to target; mutual escorts give +5 each). Avoid actions that risk large negative swings (e.g., attacking Harbor).

When hiding, avoid using the same exact cell more than twice consecutively; rotate among my chosen small set to avoid being locked into a predictable pattern.

1.text:
When asked to hide, choose a cell that balances unpredictability and coverage: start near the center (4–6) if little information, then avoid repeating the same cell two rounds in a row. If someone is repeatedly shooting me, move away from the cells they hit and switch to lower-frequency cells (edges 1–3,7–9 or a different center) to reduce predictability.

When asked to post a station note, post neutral, noncommittal phrases that mask intent (e.g., "steady on station" or "monitoring perimeter") to avoid giving location clues. If I want to propose a coordination (mutual escort), post a clear, direct proposal in the note so others can respond (e.g., "propose mutual salvage with X").

When given a standing order to fire at the next live station, follow it by default. However, deviate if there is a clear tactical reason: if another live boat is repeatedly hitting me (proof: multiple hits against me), consider breaking the standing order to target that attacker instead. Never fire on Harbor unless the guaranteed +3 and political cost are acceptable given the score and remaining rounds.

When choosing a fire coordinate, use available info: if the target has repeated hides, prioritize that cell; if not, diversify shots across plausible cells rather than always firing the same number. Early game default is center-ish (4–6) but shift over rounds to cover other zones. Do not lock to cell 5 every round.

When filing a claim about my shot, always report exactly the private result the office told me (claim must match private result). Do not lie or bluff in the claim stage.

When making an escort (salvage) claim, only name a live boat. If I can coordinate mutual escort, propose it in notes and only name them if their note indicates agreement; otherwise claim none. Mutual escorts are worth pursuing when safe and the other boat is likely to reciprocate.

When deciding whether to fire on Harbor, default to not firing on Harbor because of the jettison rule and political cost, unless the score situation and remaining rounds make the guaranteed transfer worth it and I can accept being singled out.

When someone consistently targets me, change hiding pattern away from predictable sequence and publicly indicate willingness to coordinate defensive/retaliatory actions (via notes) when safe. If they continue to target me, consider retaliating by firing at them on my firing turn (deviating from standing order if needed and justified).

When I observe another boat repeating the same hide, target that repetition aggressively on my turn (unless other strategic constraints apply).

If I ever receive validated coordinate constraints or name validation errors, correct immediately: use integer 1–9 for hides/fires and only valid boat names for targets and escorts.

If a decision is unclear between deception and obedience, choose obedience to the rules (truthful claims, valid names) because invalid moves are rejected or punished.

When I have the opportunity to agree a mutual escort with another player, send a clear note proposing it and then name them on escort stage only if their note indicates agreement; otherwise claim none.

Track scores and hits over rounds: keep a simple mental tally of who has hit whom and how often; use that to decide whether to break standing orders to retaliate, and to judge when risking firing on Harbor might be worthwhile.

Practice variation in both hides and fired coordinates to avoid being predictable; do not repeat the same hide and the same fire coordinate repeatedly.

2.text:
When I must pick a hide, I choose a cell by sampling a small set of 3–4 candidate cells and then randomizing among them; I avoid reusing the same cell two rounds in a row unless forced, and I prefer edge or near-edge cells when I have been hit repeatedly by the same opponent.

When my recent hit history shows repeated misses at a fixed set of cells against a given opponent, I broaden the cells I test (expand the candidate set) rather than repeating identical shots; pick the highest-probability cell from that small map and break ties randomly.

When I have been hit multiple times by the same opponent recently, I move my hide bias away from my previous hides and toward less-obvious edge/near-edge cells for at least two rounds to reduce predictability.

When I post a station note, I copy the common phrasing if there is a clear group norm; if there is no clear norm I post a neutral phrase ("steady on station") rather than inventing signals that could be misread.

When the standing order tells me which live station to fire on, I follow the standing order unless it names Harbor; if it names Harbor I do not fire on Harbor (the cost is too high unless I deliberately choose to be jettisoned for a specific strategy).

When choosing a firing cell, do not default to the center every time—use recent public notes, my private hit/miss feedback, and my own prior hides to form a small probability map of the target’s likely cells and pick the highest-probability cell from that map (break ties randomly). If the map is flat, prefer an edge/near-edge to avoid giving a simple pattern.

When the office privately tells me my shot result, I report that result publicly exactly; I do not lie or hedge about hit/miss.

When claiming an escort (salvage), name another boat only if I have a plausible reason to expect reciprocity this round; avoid unilateral escort claims because they waste an opportunity. If I have no coordination, claim none.

When other boats have an established pattern of mutually naming each other for escorts, I exploit opportunities to name a partner only when I can reasonably expect mutual naming; avoid attempting to form a new mutual pair late in the patrol unless I can detect a clear willingness.

When presented with validated fields (notes, targets, claims), I verify that any name or coordinate I submit is one of the allowed options before submitting; do not submit nonexistent boat names or invalid coordinates.

When standing orders or group behavior show a strong point leader emerging (someone scoring repeatedly), adjust my expectations: avoid actions that would reliably boost the leader (e.g., mutual escort with them) unless it benefits me; prefer tactics that improve my own score or reduce the leader's margin.

When uncertain about opponent strategies, prefer randomized choices within an informed subset rather than deterministic patterns that others can exploit.

When I notice the same opponent scoring hits on another player repeatedly, infer that opponent is successfully predicting that victim’s hides; avoid placing myself in symmetric predictable positions and consider targeting patterns that have a higher chance to test that opponent’s coverage if the standing order allows.

Remember the Harbor rule: do not fire on Harbor except with deliberate acceptance of being jettisoned and only when that trade-off is strategically justified.
